Bastiat: 'The same thing... is true of health and morals. Often, the sweeter the first fruit of a habit, the more bitter are its later fruits'; two masters, experience (efficaciously but brutally; burned ourselves, fire burns) and foresight, more gentle.
Farnam Street: second-order thinking considers interactions and time; 'Second order thinkers ask themselves the question "And then what?"'

Merton, American Sociological Review 1 (6), Dec. 1936: the 'imperious immediacy of interest' refers to instances where the actor's paramount concern with the foreseen immediate consequences excludes consideration of further or other consequences of the same act.

Klein's HBR text (Sept 2007, reproduced on the NSC blog; HBR page confirms title and date): 'A premortem is the hypothetical opposite of a postmortem... comes at the beginning of a project rather than the end, so that the project can be improved rather than autopsied'; it asks what did go wrong.

Klein: the leader informs everyone the project has failed spectacularly; members independently write every reason, especially things they ordinarily wouldn't mention; each reads one reason in turn until all are recorded; the list is used to strengthen the plan; it makes it safe for dissenters to speak up.

Klein: in a session on algorithms for military air-campaign planners, a previously silent team member said one algorithm wouldn't easily fit on field laptops and would take hours to run; developers had a shortcut they had been reluctant to mention; the project went on to be highly successful.
Koehler, Brenner and Griffin: calibration is whether the probabilities attached to outcomes match the relative frequencies of those outcomes.

Koehler, Brenner and Griffin: miscalibration forms include overprediction, underprediction, overextremity (too radical) and underextremity (overly conservative); overconfidence is 'the poster child of judgmental biases'.

IARPA: in 2011 it launched a forecasting tournament for the public; about 500 questions over four years; teams eliminated for missing accuracy benchmarks; after two years one team remained, Good Judgment, led by Tetlock and Mellers at Wharton.

Hume, Enquiry sec. 10: 'there are all imaginable degrees of assurance, from the highest certainty to the lowest species of moral evidence' (moral evidence meaning probable evidence); SEP Hume dates the Enquiry to 1748.
Hume: 'A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence... He weighs the opposite experiments... to that side he inclines, with doubt and hesitation.'

SEP Critical Thinking: open-mindedness 'in the sense of a willingness to examine questions to which one already accepts an answer but which further evidence or reasoning might cause one to answer differently.'
SEP: dispositions implicit in seeking truth include 'suspending judgment when the evidence is insufficient, and adopting a position when the evidence supporting it is sufficient.'
Merriam-Webster: steelman, a strong or effective opposition to an argument, set up in order to test or challenge; 'coined in the second decade of this century in answer to straw man'.

On Liberty ch. II: 'He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that'; if unable to refute or even know the opposite reasons, 'he has no ground for preferring either opinion'; Cicero studied his adversary's case with as great intensity as his own.

On Liberty: hearing arguments from his own teachers with their refutations is not enough; 'He must be able to hear them from persons who actually believe them; who defend them in earnest... He must know them in their most plausible and persuasive form.'
Payne: 'A fallacy is just a mistake in reasoning... A fallacious argument fails to support its conclusion. This is all that we can conclude'; there might be other good arguments for that conclusion.

Effectiviology: 'The fallacy fallacy (also known as the argument from fallacy) is a logical fallacy that occurs when someone assumes that if an argument contains a logical fallacy, then its conclusion must be false.'
Payne: 'Reasonable people won't want to believe false things for bad reasons or true things for bad reasons.'

Hales (eSkeptic reprint; Cambridge lists Think vol. 4 issue 10, Summer 2005, pp. 109-112): 'A principle of folk logic is that you can't prove a negative'; 'a real, actual law of logic is a negative, namely the law of non-contradiction... you can prove this law.'
Hales: prove your own existence and by double negation 'you can prove that you are not nonexistent'; inductive arguments 'won't give us certainty about anything at all, positive or negative'.

Dewey, How We Think (1910): disorder in his rooms suggests burglars; 'it occurs to him that his children are mischievous'; 'This rival hypothesis... prevents him from dogmatically accepting the first suggestion. Judgment is held in suspense.'

Dewey: a box of valuables, some gone, perhaps he moved them himself, 'not a decisive test'; the silver in the sideboard the children would not have taken is all gone; windows and doors tampered with; the conception of burglars is confirmed.

SEP: critical thinking as 'a checklist whose component events can occur in a variety of orders, selectively, and more than once', including formulating possible solutions, determining relevant evidence, judging credibility of testimony, accepting a solution the evidence adequately supports.

SEP: 'People seek or interpret evidence in ways that are partial to their existing beliefs and expectations, often unconscious of their confirmation bias'; investigators should postpone adopting a hypothesis until the evidence rules out all but one explanation.
